title: H-1B Visa Overhaul Reshapes the Rules for Indian Professionals Seeking U.S. Work Permits
excerpt: A new wage-weighted selection system replaces the random lottery, applications fall 38.5 percent, and the FY2027 cap closes with no second draw — signalling a fundamental shift in how America allocates its most sought-after work visa.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • The U.S. filled all 85,000 H-1B visa slots for FY2027, with no second lottery planned.
  • A new wage-based selection system favors higher-paid roles over random lottery selections.
  • H-1B registrations fell 38.5% year-on-year to 211,600, marking a decade-low decline.
  • 71.5% of selected beneficiaries held a U.S. advanced degree, up from 57% in FY2026.
  • Indian professionals, making up 70-75% of H-1B visas, face a transformed immigration landscape.

Key Takeaways

  • The U.S. has filled all 85,000 H-1B visa slots for FY2027, with no second lottery planned
  • A new wage-based weighted selection system replaces the random lottery, favouring higher-paid roles
  • H-1B registrations fell 38.5% year-on-year to 211,600, the sharpest decline in a decade
  • 71.5% of selected beneficiaries held a U.S. advanced degree, up from 57% in FY2026
  • Indian professionals, who account for 70-75% of H-1B visas, face a transformed playing field

The United States has closed the book on the FY2027 H-1B visa season, and the numbers tell a story of fundamental change. The U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services confirmed in early July that it had received enough petitions to fill all 85,000 available slots — 65,000 regular visas and 20,000 reserved for holders of U.S. master's degrees — with no second lottery to follow.

For the roughly 300,000 Indian professionals who depend on the H-1B programme as their primary pathway to working in America, this cycle marks a turning point that will ripple through hiring decisions, career planning, and immigration strategy for years to come.

The Lottery That Isn't Random Anymore

The most consequential shift is structural. For the first time, USCIS replaced the purely random lottery with a wage-weighted selection system that gives higher-paid positions a materially better chance of clearing the cap.

Under the new framework, registrations are weighted based on Department of Labor wage levels. A Level IV position — the highest-paid category — gets entered into the selection pool four times. Level III gets three entries, Level II gets two, and Level I gets just one. Each beneficiary still counts once against the cap, but the odds now tilt decisively toward employers offering stronger compensation.

> **""Pure randomisation does not serve the ends of the H-1B programme," the Department of Homeland Security said, adding that wage-based weighting better captures skill and economic value."**
"This weighted selection process will generally favour the allocation of H-1B visas to higher-skilled and higher-paid aliens, while maintaining the opportunity for employers to secure H-1B workers at all wage levels," the Department of Homeland Security said in the final rule.

The results are already visible. USCIS data shows that 71.5 percent of selected beneficiaries for FY2027 held a U.S. advanced degree, up sharply from 57 percent in FY2026. Only 17.7 percent of selected registrations came from the lowest wage category, signalling a clear pivot away from entry-level and staffing-model positions.

A Sharp Drop in Applications

The FY2027 cycle also saw demand fall off a cliff. According to USCIS data released in May, just 211,600 valid registrations were submitted — a 38.5 percent decline from the 343,981 received for FY2026. While the agency has not published a final selection rate, the drop suggests the new rules are already filtering out speculative applications and registrations from employers less willing to commit to higher wages.

Employers whose registrations were selected during the initial lottery had until June 30 to submit complete petitions. Successful applicants will be eligible to begin working in the United States from October 1, the start of the new fiscal year.

What This Means for Indian Professionals

Indians account for roughly 70 to 75 percent of H-1B visas issued annually, making them by far the largest beneficiary group. The wage-weighted system creates clear winners and losers within this community.

Experienced professionals, senior engineers, and workers in specialised roles at major technology firms are likely to benefit. Their positions typically fall into higher wage levels, giving them substantially better odds under the new system. Google, Microsoft, Amazon, and other large employers already offer compensation well above Level I thresholds.

The losers are equally clear. Entry-level roles, positions at IT consulting and staffing firms, and lower-paid jobs that previously had an equal shot under the random lottery now face significantly worse odds. The Indian IT services sector — companies that historically filed large volumes of H-1B petitions at lower wage levels — will feel the squeeze most acutely.

Broader Uncertainty Compounds the Pressure

The lottery redesign arrives amid a broader tightening of the U.S. immigration apparatus. The government has expanded social media and online presence checks to all visa applicants worldwide, leading to longer processing times. Several major technology companies, including Google and Apple, have reportedly cautioned employees on work visas against international travel due to the risk of extended delays at consulates.

A new $100,000 additional fee for certain H-1B petitions, introduced alongside the wage-weighted system, has added another layer of cost for employers. Compliance requirements have also stiffened, with companies now required to declare wage levels, job codes, and work locations at the registration stage itself.

"Pure randomisation does not serve the ends of the H-1B programme," the Department of Homeland Security said, adding that wage-based weighting better captures skill and economic value.

The Road Ahead

For Indian professionals already in the United States on H-1B visas, the immediate impact is limited — existing visa holders are not affected by the new selection rules. But for those entering the pipeline, the message is clear: the path to an American work visa now runs through higher compensation, not higher volume.

Immigration attorneys say the combination of the wage-weighted system, increased fees, and tighter vetting amounts to a fundamental reorientation of the H-1B programme. What was once a lottery is now, in effect, a market — and the price of entry has gone up.
